query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minute amount of Nb or Ti as a controlled nanoscale interfacial dopant will induce the formation of coherent, ductile precipitates at the internal lamellar boundaries, thereby arresting microcrack propagation and simultaneously enhancing both yield strength and room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies that have numerous vulnerable internal boundaries susceptible to microcrack initiation.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a microalloying addition of Nb or Ti during processing and apply an optimized heat-treatment to promote the formation of coherent, nanoscale interfacial precipitates.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation with controlled dopant concentration and heat-treatment conditions that ensure precipitates remain nanoscale and coherent.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent nanoscale precipitates at the internal boundaries of lamellar colonies.
generation.mechanism: The precipitates contribute to precipitation strengthening while also acting as barriers that deflect or arrest microcrack propagation, thus improving both strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples treated with the dopant are expected to show higher yield strength and an increased amount of plastic deformation (i.e., improved ductility) compared to the unmodified baseline.
generation.baseline: The unmodified lamellar-colony alloy produced via conventional processing, which exhibits microcrack initiation at internal boundaries and limited tensile ductility.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are contingent on maintaining the precipitate size in the nanoscale regime and ensuring their coherency; excessive precipitate coarsening or incoherence will negate the improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal dopant concentration and precise processing window to achieve the desired nanoscale precipitate formation are not yet fully determined, and the improvements may vary depending on the specific alloy composition.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate several batches of alloy samples with varying concentrations of Nb or Ti and subject them to a controlled heat-treatment aimed at producing nanoscale coherent precipitates. Conduct room-temperature tensile tests and utilize transmission electron microscopy to assess precipitate size, coherency, and microcrack formation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If doped samples do not exhibit statistically significant increases in both yield strength and tensile ductility compared to the unmodified baseline, or if the precipitates are found to coarsen and lose coherency, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

prior_attempts: A wide range of microstructural-design and processing strategies, including adjustments in cooling rates, phase fraction tailoring, and grain refinement, have been attempted but did not eliminate the room-temperature brittleness.
These methods generally improved strength but still suffered from insufficient tensile ductility due to persistent microcracking.
frame.understanding: the role of interfacial engineering in mitigating microcrack nucleation and propagation in dual-phase lamellar structures
frame.testable_hypothesis: Introducing a controlled nanoscale interfacial dopant—such as microalloying with Nb or Ti—that promotes the formation of coherent, ductile precipitates at the internal boundaries will simultaneously enhance tensile strength (via precipitation strengthening) and ductility (by arresting or deflecting microcrack propagation). Relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony alloy, the doped alloy will exhibit higher yield strength and an extended plastic deformation range before failure. The beneficial effect is expected to be limited to conditions where the precipitates remain coherent and finely dispersed; should the precipitate size exceed a critical threshold or if the interfacial structure becomes incoherent, the intervention will no longer improve the balance of properties. Previous work on tempered martensitic steels and dual-phase steels has shown that nanoscale interfacial precipitates can delay crack initiation and improve toughness. An experiment to falsify this hypothesis would involve fabricating alloy samples with a range of dopant concentrations and optimized heat-treatment parameters to achieve the targeted nanoscale precipitate distribution, followed by room-temperature tensile testing and electron microscopy. If samples do not exhibit a measurable improvement in both tensile ductility and strength beyond a predefined benchmark relative to the baseline, the hypothesis would be refuted.

decision.trend: Early work on eutectic high‐entropy alloys (e.g. PMC4145285) focused on processing routes—adjusting cooling rates, phase fraction tailoring, and grain refinement—to achieve high strength, but these methods consistently left the internal lamellar interfaces vulnerable to microcrack initiation, thereby limiting room‐temperature ductility. Later studies (such as PMC10213035) began to explore the benefits of introducing fine, coherent precipitates in dual‐phase systems via stepwise thermo‐mechanical treatments. These approaches verified that when the interfaces between the phases are engineered to be coherent and finely dispersed, dislocation activity can be favorably modified and crack propagation delayed. However, while these efforts improved strength and ductility in other alloy systems, a direct intervention at the internal boundaries of eutectic lamellar colonies to arrest microcrack nucleation has not been fully exploited.
decision.unsolved: No single processing or compositional strategy has yet been demonstrated to simultaneously enhance both room-temperature tensile ductility and strength in eutectic high-entropy alloys by specifically targeting and fortifying the vulnerable internal colony interfaces. The key remaining challenge is to mitigate microcrack nucleation and propagation at these internal boundaries without compromising the overall phase architecture.
decision.lever: introduce a controlled nanoscale interfacial dopant (e.g., a microalloying addition of Nb or Ti) that promotes the formation of coherent, ductile interfacial precipitates
decision.why: This approach directly targets the internal boundaries where microcracking initiates. It builds on the evolving trend from merely refining global microstructure to engineering interfacial cohesion. Prior evidence from tempered martensitic steels and dual-phase alloys shows that nanoscale, coherent precipitates can arrest crack propagation and improve both strength (via precipitation strengthening) and ductility (by deflecting or arresting microcracks). By precisely tuning dopant concentration and heat-treatment parameters to maintain fine, coherent precipitates, this intervention is the most logical next step to overcome the brittle behavior of unmodified lamellar colonies.
